notes.meaning: Ezekiel tells us that this message came from the LORD. It was not his own idea. The chapter has three parts: a picture-story (verses 1-10), its meaning (verses 11-21), and a promise about God's coming King (verses 22-24).

God tells Ezekiel to give the people a riddle and a parable, which is a story that makes a comparison. The goal was not to confuse them. A riddle grabs attention, makes people think, and sticks in the memory. These hard-hearted listeners might ignore plain words, but a puzzle could wake them up.

The great eagle is Nebuchadnezzar, the mighty king of Babylon. His huge wings show how far his empire reached. His many-colored feathers stand for the many nations and languages under his rule. Lebanon stands for Jerusalem, with its palace full of cedar wood. The cedar is David's royal family, and its top is King Jehoiachin.

The eagle snaps off the top shoot and carries it to a land of traders. That land is Babylon, a great center of trade. Young King Jehoiachin, only eighteen and king for just three months, was taken there with his princes. A king from David's line now had to live among merchants. He had to make the best of it.

Next the eagle plants a seed from the land itself. This is Zedekiah, Jehoiachin's uncle, a native prince and not a foreign ruler. He was set like a willow by plenty of water. A willow grows well in a wet place, but no one expects it to become a grand tree.

The plant becomes a low, spreading vine instead of a tall cedar. Judah could still do well, but it would no longer stand tall among the nations. Its branches turned toward the eagle, showing Zedekiah's loyalty to Babylon. Its roots stayed under the eagle, because Judah's safety depended on Babylon.

A second great eagle appears. This is the king of Egypt. He is strong, but his empire is not as wide as Babylon's. The vine longs for him and reaches its roots and branches toward him, hoping he will water it. Egypt watered its fields through ditches from the Nile. The sad thing is that the vine already had plenty of water where it was planted.

God repeats that the vine had been planted in good soil by plenty of water. Zedekiah was not starving or cruelly treated. If he had stayed faithful, his kingdom could have lasted and done well. His turning away came from pride and ingratitude, not need.

God asks, "Will it flourish?" The answer is no. The first eagle, Babylon, will pull it up and strip its fruit, which points to Zedekiah's children. Its fresh leaves will wither in the middle of springtime. It will be easy work, because God himself hands the vine over. God does not need a huge army to carry out his plans.

Even if the vine is replanted, it will not last. The hot, dry east wind stands for Babylon, whose armies came from the east. The vine will wither in the very bed where it was given every chance. In fact, Zedekiah was caught near Jericho, on his own soil.
Now God gives the meaning of the riddle in plain words. The puzzle had caught the people's attention. Now they are ready for the lesson. By explaining it clearly, God leaves them without excuse.

God calls Israel a "rebellious house" and asks if they really don't understand. It is a rebuke, because anyone who knew recent events could have solved the riddle. The eagle's act is explained: the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and took King Jehoiachin and his officials to Babylon.

Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah king and bound him with a covenant, a binding agreement. Zedekiah swore by the God of Israel to stay loyal. The leading men were taken away, partly as hostages and partly to weaken the land. Judah would be kept low, but it could stand safely if it kept the agreement. The terms were open and fair, so Zedekiah had no excuse.

Zedekiah rebelled anyway. He secretly sent messengers to Egypt asking for horses and soldiers. God's law had warned Israel's kings not to go back to Egypt for horses. Three times now God asks if such a man can succeed. Even people who did not know God believed that oath-breakers would not escape.

God makes a solemn promise by his own life. Zedekiah will die in Babylon, the home of the king he betrayed. That came true: his eyes were put out, and he was taken to Babylon and never came home. He ended up with far worse servitude than the kind he had tried to escape.

Pharaoh's great army will be no real help when Babylon builds ramps and siege walls around Jerusalem. An Egyptian army did come, and the Babylonians left for a while to meet it. But Egypt was pushed back, and the siege went on. God often weakens the human strength we lean on in place of him.
Zedekiah "gave his hand," a solemn sign of making a promise. Then he broke it. Because he made an oath before the LORD and then despised it, he took God's name lightly. So he will not escape.

God calls the oath and covenant "My oath" and "My covenant," because Zedekiah swore them in the LORD's name. Breaking faith with Nebuchadnezzar was breaking faith with God. God cares about honesty between people, even with those who do not worship him. Truth is a debt we owe to everyone.

God says he will throw his own net over Zedekiah. Babylon's army was simply God's net. Nebuchadnezzar acted for his own reasons, but God was in control. Zedekiah would be judged for betraying God. That judgment began at Riblah, where his sons were killed before his eyes, and finished in Babylon.

Zedekiah's soldiers will run and fall by the sword, and the rest will be scattered in every direction. This happened when the city wall was broken and the men of war fled. "All" here means most of them, not every last one. The people would not listen to warnings, so they would learn the truth of God's word by living through it.

Now comes good news. God himself will do what the eagle tried to do, and do it far better. He will take a tender shoot from the top of David's family tree. That shoot is the Messiah, God's promised King. "Tender" shows his humble beginnings. He will be planted on a high mountain, which means Zion, the center of God's kingdom.

differ.view: The promise is fulfilled in Christ's church. His kingdom began small after the return from exile and keeps growing until he comes again on the last day.
The kingdom began when the exiles returned and fully began with Christ's first coming. It will be seen at its highest when Christ returns to reign from Zion over the whole earth.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read this as Ezekiel's hope that David's royal family would be restored to rule a renewed Israel. They see it as the prophet's hope for Israel more than a direct picture of Jesus.

notes.meaning: The little shoot grows into a majestic cedar on Israel's mountain. Birds of every kind come to nest in its shade. That stands for people from every nation, Jews and non-Jews alike, finding safety under Christ. It is like Jesus' parable of the tiny mustard seed that becomes a great tree.

The "trees of the field" are the kings and kingdoms of the earth. They will all learn that God brings down the proud and lifts up the lowly, as Hannah and Mary later sang. Mighty Babylon would fall, and David's house, which looked dead, would flourish again in Christ. When God says it, it is as good as done.
